newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: KL shares end lower on cash calls, foreign selling.
newsitem.headline: KL shares end lower on cash calls, foreign selling.

text.p: Malaysian shares fell to a seven-and-a-half month low on Monday after leveraged retail investors were asked to top up their portfolios wth cash, and a foreign institutional sell-off, dealers and analysts said.
At the close, the benchmark Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks fell 37.27 points, or 3.27 percent, to 1,101.09.

"There's a general downrating of Malaysia by foreign institutions on the perception that earnings growth among banks and property companies will slow down," said Ramlan Ahmad, senior manager at fund managers Commerce MGI.
Malaysia's central bank announced measures in late March to curb lending to the property sector for speculative purposes.
"Foreign institutions want to get out, but they can't. There are no buyers," said a dealer at a local bank-backed brokerage house.
"The market is reacting to Wall Street's fall on Friday, but locally it's margin calls that are affecting the market," said Ooi Soon Beng, head of research at Inter-Pacific Securities.
Sime Darby fell 50 cents to 7.70 ringgit, while MBf Capital dropped 20 to 3.88. Both companies have large exposures to the property market, said analysts.
Fund managers said they were using the fall as an opportunity to buy quality blue-chip stocks.
"We're not panicking here," said Robert Coombe, executive director at Commerce Asset Fund Managers. "If you're not geared and not in the Second Board, you should be buying," he added.

"With a prospective 1997 p.e. (price-earnings multiple) of around 18 times, you can't go wrong," said Ramlan. The Kuala Lumpur stock market has historically traded at a p.e. of between 20 and 21 times, analysts said.
The market would take around two to three months to recover, said Ramlan. "A lot of players got wounded. They will take time to heal."

The resignation of Malaysia's Selangor state chief minister on Saturday added to the market's angst, analysts and dealers said. The state's investment arm controls several small-capitalised listed companies, said the head of research at a local brokerage house.
Market volume stood at 269 million shares, valued at 2.01 billion ringgit. Losers trounced gainers 711 to 21.

"No volume is a good sign," said Ang Kok Heng, general manager of T.A. Asset Management. "I think the market is coming to a bottom, but it's hard to say if a sharp technical rebound will come in. If the Dow stabilises, but doesn't rebound, I think the market will be sideways."

At the close on the Kuala Lumpur Options and Financial Futures Exchange, the spot April contract shed 30 points to settle at 1,102.0 with 608 lots traded. The May futures contract slipped 27.7 to 1,101.5 with six lots changing hands.
